site.title: Tyler for Esquimalt
site.description: Tyler Russell is running for Esquimalt Township Council. A safer, more fun, easier-to-move-around, low-cortisol Esquimalt. General voting day is Saturday, October 17, 2026.
site.votingHeading: General voting day is Saturday, October 17, 2026.
site.votingText: Advance voting days and polling places are set by the Township. Check [esquimalt.ca](https://www.esquimalt.ca) for dates, locations and what to bring.
site.landAck: Esquimalt is on the traditional territory of the lək̓ʷəŋən‑speaking peoples, known today as the Songhees Nation and the Xʷsepsəm (Esquimalt) Nation, who have cared for this land and water since time immemorial. We live, work and play here as their guests.

hero.lead: Safer, more fun, easier to get around, and filled with even more love and inclusion than it already is. A town whose very design says *you belong here* to the people living in it now, to newcomers, and to the generations yet to come.

letter.body:
My name is Tyler Russell and I am running to be your township councillor.

I want to build upon the work of Mayor Barb Desjardins and the current council and make Esquimalt even safer, more fun, more accessible, easier to move around in, and filled with more love and inclusion than it already is.

I imagine a low‑cortisol town, one that has, embedded in its design, a communication of love to its current citizens, its newcomers, and future generations. Here is what I want to do to get us there.
letter.signTagline: Saxe Point neighbour, dad of an almost‑five‑year‑old, apartment dweller, car share and transit user

platform.heading: Ten things I want to do
platform.intro: These are my starting points. The door‑to‑door conversations happening now will sharpen them, and I'll post what changes and why.

items.title: Fix the daily traffic jam
items.text: Fix the horrible daily traffic jam that much of our town has become.
items.linkLabel: First proposal: the Esquimalt Free Ride pilot →

items.title: Grow the places where we play
items.text: Enhance the delightful zones and facilities where children, and our whole community, can roam, connect, learn and play.

items.title: Make it easier to walk and ride
items.text: Increase the walkability and transit‑ability of our community.

items.title: Calm the car‑and‑people zones
items.text: Reduce the stress of the car‑pedestrian, car‑child and car‑cyclist interface zones.

items.title: Honour the Songhees and Xʷsepsəm Nations
items.text: Increasingly honour the lək̓ʷəŋən‑speaking peoples, the Songhees Nation and the Xʷsepsəm (Esquimalt) Nation, on whose land we live, work and play, while deepening collaboration between the Township and both Nations.

items.title: Pace development with infrastructure
items.text: Keep new development in line with the roads, pipes, parks and services that have to support it.

items.title: Become a carbon‑removing town
items.text: In addition to emissions reduction, enhance green space and managed community biomass production, and move toward pyrolysis, enhanced rock weathering and other technologies in our green‑waste management, city works and urban design, so Esquimalt removes more carbon from the atmosphere than it puts in.

items.title: Bring in more outside investment
items.text: Work with staff to increase the grant funding, philanthropy and other external investment that goes into enhancing our community.

items.title: Bring in a right to cool
items.text: Table a bylaw, as New Westminster has done, so that every rental home has at least one room that stays at 26°C or lower during heatwaves. Tenants should not have to endure dangerous indoor heat.
items.linkLabel: Proposal 02: a Right to Cool bylaw →

items.title: Leave it better than we found it
items.text: Leave our town safer, more inclusive, more bountiful, and universally smile‑filled than we found it.

voice.heading: Before anything else, I will stand for your voice being heard.
voice.intro: Over the next few weeks I'm going door to door asking two questions: what is your immediate concern, and what is your long‑term vision for Esquimalt? Here is what happens with your answers.
steps: I compile what I hear and post it on this site, so you can see what your neighbours are saying.
We turn it into a council‑ready report.
Where there are solutions, we draft proposals for council's consideration.
I mark the ones I will personally push for so you always know where I stand.
voice.formHeading: Can't wait for the knock? Send it now.
voice.concernPlaceholder: The thing that stresses you out about living here right now.
voice.visionPlaceholder: Esquimalt in ten years, if it went the way you hoped.
voice.formNote: Goes straight to Tyler's inbox. Nothing is published from this form; themes may appear on this page, never names.
voice.formNoteMailto: This opens your email app with your answers filled in. Nothing is stored on this site.

hearing.heading: At the door, so far
hearing.intro: Updated as the door‑knocking goes. Concerns are grouped by theme and never attributed to a person by name. The theme cards are the running tally; the dispatches below them are the full write‑ups.

cards.title: Child care
cards.text: Not enough spots, with young children on multiple waitlists. Nothing for parents who work evenings and weekends. Hardest on new immigrant families with few local networks.

cards.title: Street parking
cards.meta: Days one and two at the door
cards.text: Homefront spots are fiercely valued, and residents fear a big construction project would squeeze them out. Some suspect out‑of‑town commuters park here to bike downtown. Resident‑only parking on affected streets is worth a look.

cards.title: Bike lanes on Lampson
cards.text: Nearly everyone with a concern is a cyclist and supports the lanes; the objection is the concrete barriers. I'll check with first responders first, then review how the lanes are working with cyclists, drivers and residents.

cards.title: Policing costs and a regional plan
cards.text: Esquimalt shares VicPD's costs with Victoria while neighbours run their own forces. Decades of studies, no stable regional plan. I'll move to convene the neighbouring councils and police boards.

cards.title: Getting to and from the base
cards.meta: Days one and two at the door
cards.text: Base parking is free because Esquimalt's is. Residents miss the Blue Boat, which carried about 500 base workers a day. I'll ask base leadership what stands in the way of a base‑employee shuttle.

cards.title: The right to cool
cards.text: A bylaw so every rental unit has at least one room at 26°C or lower on hot nights, and tenants can always use their own cooling. New Westminster has one. See Proposal 02.

cards.title: Community stake in developments
cards.text: Two recent projects compared by one resident. Where the community had a stake, an old tree stayed and the space breathes.

cards.title: Small fixes
cards.meta: Days one and two at the door
cards.text: Stop signs at Munro and Fraser. Traffic calming on Sturdee. Speed bumps in the Ellery–Colville laneway where kids play. A yellow‑line audit. Consult professional drivers on traffic changes.

cards.title: Community safety beyond policing
cards.text: Food, company, mental‑health and addiction support, and a place to belong make a town safer too. Rainbow Kitchen and the United Church at Admirals and Lyall show how.

cards.title: Building heights and the OCP
cards.text: One chorus: keep to the Official Community Plan, six storeys where the plan says six. Density has support. Departures from the plan do not.

cards.title: Living beside construction
cards.text: Years of noise and blasting wear people down. I'll knock on doors around proposed developments, and push for prefabrication and construction plans that care for the actual neighbours.

cards.title: Green for grey
cards.text: Density in one place, more green in another: parkland through DCCs, amenities through ACCs, canopy through tree rules. See Proposal 03.

cards.title: Time as accessibility
cards.text: Double the posted parking time for accessible‑permit holders, as the Australian state of Victoria does. Low cost, and worth championing region‑wide.

cards.title: Housing and a coalition of the pro‑active
cards.text: Esquimalt should stay pro‑active on the right to housing, and no municipality should sit out. I'll work to gather councillors, churches and grassroots groups across the region around tangible solutions.

cards.title: Shortcut traffic
cards.text: Drivers dodging the jam cut through Old Esquimalt Road and the Ellery–Colville laneway. Speed bumps are welcome but not enough. Fix the jam itself and the shortcuts lose their appeal.

cards.title: Property taxes and seniors
cards.text: Taxes are too high, and the Province's deferment changes (prime plus 2%, compounded monthly) land hardest on seniors with fixed incomes. Keep pushing the Province for an income‑tested fix, and advertise the Township's ten‑month payment plan.

cards.title: A $10,000 drain connection
cards.text: A young couple with a flooding basement was quoted $10,000 to connect a perimeter drain. Council's 2021 program says work on private pipes is shared equally; nobody can find who qualifies. Publish the rules, and let owners pay the fee over time on the tax bill.

cards.title: Archie Browning
cards.text: Finish the upgrades sooner rather than later, so kids can skate regularly.

cards.title: Sidewalks
cards.text: The common ground between bike‑lane lovers and bike‑lane haters. Where new sidewalks went in, both camps call them a wonderful addition, for child safety above all.

cards.title: Get the cars moving again
cards.text: One neighbour's commute went from 7 minutes to 30. Bring back a Blue Boat‑style service for base staff, and put transit that pulls real drivers off the road ahead of bike lanes.

cards.title: A Viewfield station
cards.text: Rail only works when daily life is built around the stations. With the Victoria–Langford corridor under study, plan a Viewfield station neighbourhood: a place to live, work, make things and shop, connected to the region by rail.

cards.title: Who pays for infrastructure
cards.text: Esquimalt passed its five‑year housing target in two years with no amenity cost charge in place. Pace development with infrastructure, and have developers, not taxpayers, carry the cost.

cards.title: Beach fires and a beat cop
cards.text: Longing for the days of beach fires, and for an officer walking the streets, last seen nearly 20 years ago.

cards.title: Housing the unhoused
cards.text: Access to housing for the unhoused too often gets left on the back burner. Neighbours want to see meaningful action.

cards.title: Roadside gardening
cards.text: Food gardens on boulevards and public land bring nourishment, healing and connection. Victoria publishes boulevard gardening guidelines; Esquimalt could borrow them.

dispatches.title: Sidewalks are where we all get along
dispatches.summary: Common ground between bike‑lane lovers and haters, why the Dayliner didn't work, a Viewfield station, who pays for infrastructure, housing the unhoused, and the beauty of roadside gardening.
dispatches.body:
If I were to describe Esquimalt politics in terms of camps, you could basically say there are bike‑lane lovers and bike‑lane haters. On Saturday I think I found our community's most common common ground. I thought it would be traffic, but not quite: people who own cargo bikes and mostly bike rarely mention concerns with traffic, though people who bike some of the time, and love the lanes, definitely do. The real common ground between the lovers and the haters is sidewalks! In an area where new sidewalks went in, people at both ends of the Esquimalt political spectrum told me what a wonderful addition they have been. What they have done for child safety was gratefully noted by multiple parties.

Sidewalks are where we all get along!

## Get the cars moving again

One sidewalk‑loving neighbour had a very concise request: get rid of the bike lanes and put the speed limit back up to 50. You've got to get the cars moving again! If you want to save the environment, you can't have everyone idling for two hours a day. What was once a 7‑minute commute for them is now 30.

I don't share every part of that prescription, but the frustration is real, and what they said next is hard to argue with.

They hugely support bringing back some kind of Blue Boat service, and reminisced about how it worked: where the parking lots were on the Colwood and Langford side, the friends who really enjoyed it, how fast the crossing was. They had little patience for studies for studies' sake, like [the one done some years ago](https://cheknews.ca/snc-lavalin-pre-feasibility-study-outlines-potential-west-shore-passenger-ferry-544198/) exploring the possibility of a general public ferry when, as we all know, what matters is a service for base staff.

They insisted that investment in transit should come before bike lanes, because as they see it an effective transit system can pull real drivers off the road.

## Why the Dayliner didn't work

They remembered the old Via Rail Dayliner, which ran out of Victoria through Langford and up‑island, and how hardly anyone rode it because life wasn't organised around it. People still had to get groceries and everything else, and those services were available via car, they emphasised, so the Dayliner didn't make sense for daily life.

I agree. If you want people to use a mode of transit, the city around it has to be designed with some sensitivity to normal ways of life. Very pragmatic folk, they support a long‑term light rail vision so long as it isn't a white elephant irrelevant to daily life. I shared my experience living in Korea and Japan, where grocery stores and all kinds of everyday needs are built into and around stations, and how places like Hong Kong have built a whole city around transit. It takes the long‑term application of those design principles to make that kind of system work, not a one‑off project in a sea of design principles that think otherwise.

The timing matters. Last December the Songhees and Xʷsepsəm Nations, the CRD and five municipalities, Esquimalt among them, [agreed to explore together](https://www.crd.ca/media/file/2025-12-11-mr-lekwungen-nations-and-local-mayors-pursue-shared-vision-island-rail-corridorpdf) the future of the rail corridor between Victoria and Langford, under the Nations' leadership. In March the CRD board committed $1.7 million it had held in reserve for the corridor since 2012, as [Victoria News reported](https://vicnews.com/2026/03/11/crd-pledges-decade-old-1-7m-grant-to-island-reconciliation-corridor-initiative/), and study work is under way. On Wednesday, here in Esquimalt, the federal government [added $500,000](https://www.canada.ca/en/pacific-economic-development/news/2026/09/pacifican-invests-in-passenger-rail-opportunities-connecting-victoria-west-and-langford.html) for the Island Corridor Foundation's feasibility study. It is a study, not a train. But it comes exactly at the moment when we need to start shifting our urban design concepts if we are going to be serious about this.

## A Viewfield station

In Esquimalt, I see a Viewfield station, right next to Wholesale Club, Flying Squirrel and Driftwood Brewing, as a ready‑made super station. Creative zoning could allow housing density there while keeping it an industrial and employment zone, turning it into an integrated employment neighbourhood: a place to live, work, play, make things, shop and connect to the rest of the region by rail.

Making an adjustment like that to our OCP would mark a larger shift in how we think about Esquimalt. Twentieth‑century car‑oriented planning separated cities into residential, commercial and industrial districts. Development around rail stations gives us a chance to integrate compatible uses again and build complete neighbourhoods with mobility at their core. With a comprehensive review of the Official Community Plan expected to start in the next council's term, these are ideas we can start thinking about together.

If we lean into rail‑oriented design, the economic potential around future station areas is tremendous. I can imagine the Naden, Viewfield and Vic West terminus stations together becoming a vibrant regional centre of economic and social life by 2050.

That is a long‑term vision. But we also have an immediate problem: getting people moving again. That means measures we can act on much sooner: reviving a Blue Boat‑style service, improving transit access, as with my [Esquimalt Free Ride](#proposal-01) proposal, and making transit schedules actually work for the shifts of the thousands of people travelling to and from Esquimalt every day.

We need to solve the congestion of today while designing for the Esquimalt of 2050.

Another neighbour mentioned that some of the traffic‑calming measures have people dangerously jumping lanes just to get out of an intersection.

## Who pays for infrastructure

One neighbour longed for the days of beach fires, and reckons the last time they saw a beat cop walking Esquimalt's streets was nearly 20 years ago. They work in construction and like development, but feel that here in Esquimalt, there may have been a bit much of late, especially when, as they see it, the burden of infrastructure is passed on to taxpayers. They were aghast that Esquimalt has no amenity cost charge or equivalent in place to make sure developers pay for the infrastructure their projects need.

They knew that when the Province announced its five‑year housing target of 754 new homes for Esquimalt back in 2024, Esquimalt went on to blow past it by more than 200 homes in just two years, with much more still in the pipeline. The Township's latest [report to the Province](https://www.esquimalt.ca/media/file/housing-target-progress-report-2026) counts 989 homes completed and another 427 approved and on the way. Again they emphasised pacing development with infrastructure. We can't let infrastructure founder.

The [CRD's own projections](https://www.crd.ca/media/file/appendix-b-population-projection-analysispdf) show the region's population growth slowing, largely because of federal immigration policy. Given the correlation between population growth and housing demand, it is sad to think we may be late in bringing in a charge that speaks to Esquimalt's real infrastructure deficit.

Finding a way to close that deficit will be one of the big challenges for the next council. Frankly, the answer will not come from small levies on a fourplex or sixplex here and there, and it certainly should not come from further tax increases. It should come from having development and amenity cost charges in place, as I propose in my [Green for Grey](#proposal-03) initiative, and from realising larger initiatives like, for example, a Viewfield station neighbourhood. That vision needs federal, provincial, First Nations, regional and neighbouring governments pulling together. The [coalition agreement](https://www.crd.ca/media/file/2025-12-11-mr-lekwungen-nations-and-local-mayors-pursue-shared-vision-island-rail-corridorpdf) the Nations, the CRD and five municipalities, Esquimalt among them, signed last December is a good start. The job is to make sure that realising it also relieves our infrastructure deficit, without further shocks to taxpayers.

## A garden on the commons

My last conversation of the evening was with a neighbour tending a guerrilla garden on a patch of public land. At first they said their mind was too caught up in international affairs. Then they voiced concern about access to housing for the unhoused, how it too often gets left on the back burner, and how much they would like to see meaningful action.

Then they shared a beautiful history of guerrilla gardening and seed sharing: how the Victoria Seed Library came to be, with strong Esquimalt participation, and how transforming rough lawn on municipal land into a luscious food patch brought personal healing and rich community connection. They spoke with wonder of the expanse between Esquimalt High and the road: "You could grow a lot of food there!!" They described the empowerment of growing food not just for yourself in your own back yard, but on a community commons. It provides year‑round nourishment and a path to social connection, fostering a culture of respect for labour and care, and joy on both sides of acts of sharing bounty, sometimes including with the deer.

They volunteered that they may have capacity to help promote more front‑yard and roadside gardening, and were invigorated by what that could mean for our community. I was delighted, and said that if I am elected I may reach out to see what is possible. Victoria publishes [boulevard gardening guidelines](https://www.victoria.ca/media/file/boulevard-gardening-guidelines) that tell residents what they can plant and where. I could not find an Esquimalt equivalent. That would be an easy one to borrow.

An afternoon and evening of seeing the breadth of possibility in our community. With neighbours like these, we have a lot we can do together and a beautiful future to look forward to!

dispatches.title: Traffic and Taxes
dispatches.summary: Shortcuts through Old Esquimalt Road, property taxes and what the deferment changes mean for seniors, and a $10,000 quote to connect a drain.
dispatches.body:
With the traffic congestion of recent years, people are gunning for alternative routes. I mentioned earlier a neighbour's concern about drivers ripping through the laneway between Ellery and Colville. On Friday I spoke with people worried about Old Esquimalt Road being used the same way. They were grateful for the speed bumps, but said the bumps aren't having enough impact.

I am not above taking detours myself. Around 3:30 one recent afternoon, I went down Grenville to avoid the jammed‑up Admirals and Esquimalt intersection. It is not something to be proud of, but it was definitely faster.

That is the point. The traffic situation is raising our community's cortisol levels and pushing people into traffic‑evading manoeuvres through streets that were never meant for them. Speed bumps treat the symptom. Addressing the jam itself, as I propose, is key.

One neighbour gratefully acknowledged the difference the pedestrian crossings on Esquimalt Road have made. Another wants more enforcement at those crossings; they have been dismayed time and again by drivers not slowing down, for seniors in particular. Enforcement may help. But in my opinion the root cause is people who are stressed and in a rush because the streets are jammed everywhere else.

There was a lot of appetite for any proposal that would ease the traffic.

## Property taxes

A few neighbours commented (or maybe that is too gentle a word) about property taxes! One was livid with the current council, first for, as they put it, all but banning cars. They had noticed traffic counters on Old Esquimalt Road and suspected that meant more bike lanes. They weren't against bike lanes altogether, as one particular Esquimalt chorus sings; they were against the concrete‑barriered kind, and feared those, or some other anti‑car measure, were coming for their street. I don't know what the counters are for. I will ask. But the real boil came with property taxes: they are too high, and something has to be done about them!

Another neighbour focused on what taxes mean for seniors on low or fixed incomes. If you retired in the last couple of years expecting to live another thirty, and you just watched property taxes jump *and* the rules for deferring them change, it is understandably scary. These are not increases anyone could have planned for.

The deferment change is the quiet one. Until this year, a senior deferring their property taxes paid simple interest at prime minus 2%. Under the 2026 provincial budget it is now prime plus 2%, compounded monthly. Here is the [BC Seniors Advocate's release](https://www.seniorsadvocatebc.ca/app/uploads/sites/4/2026/05/nr-property-tax-deferment-changes.pdf) and the [Province's own explainer](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/taxes/property-taxes/annual-property-tax/property-tax-deferment-program/tax-deferment-interest-fees). Staying in your home just got more expensive for the people least able to absorb it.

## So what can be done?

One bit of good news: Esquimalt council brought resolution NR51, "Changes to Provincial Property Tax Deferment Program," to the Union of BC Municipalities convention, which wrapped up on Friday. It urges the Province to review the changes "with consideration for the needs of low‑income seniors on fixed incomes, including the introduction of an income threshold, so that the program continues to support low‑income seniors as originally intended." You can read it in the [UBCM Resolutions Book](https://www.ubcm.ca/sites/default/files/2026-08/2026%20UBCM%20Resolutions%20Book.pdf) (search for NR51) or in [Esquimalt's own report](https://esquimalt.ca.legistar.com/ViewReport.ashx?M=R&N=Text&GID=5&ID=37306&GUID=3277B2EA-CBB8-4B14-8FB3-64A7744DDF32&Title=Legislation+Text).

Thankfully it passed. Credit where it is due. Now we need to keep up the push until there is a program in place that works for seniors.

BC municipalities don't have the power to act alone on this the way Toronto does. But Toronto's approach is worth looking at. Its [Property Tax Increase Cancellation Program](https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/property-taxes-utilities/property-tax/property-tax-water-solid-waste-relief-and-rebate-programs/property-tax-and-utility-relief-program/) lets low‑income seniors and low‑income people with disabilities apply to have their tax *increase* cancelled. For 2026 that means a household income of $62,000 or less, a home assessed under $975,000, and being over 65, or 60 to 64 and receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement, or receiving disability benefits. That is the kind of targeted tool I would want Esquimalt asking the Province for.

What Esquimalt can do today: the Township already has a [pre‑authorized payment plan](https://www.esquimalt.ca/government-bylaws/taxes-grants/property-tax/pre-payment) that spreads property taxes over ten monthly payments, August to May. Nobody I spoke with knew about it. It should be far better advertised, and it has a gap: you have to be fully paid up before you can join, which is no help to someone already stretched. It is a stopgap, not a fix, but a stopgap that spares someone a July cash crunch is worth having.

## A $10,000 drain

One young couple told me their basement has flooded repeatedly. The fix is a perimeter drain connected to the municipal storm drain. The Township's quote to connect: $10,000. That is $5,000 for the connection and up to $5,000 more for traffic control because they are on a busy road. For them, that means it just can't happen. This is troubling. Constant moisture has serious implications for health, and for the house itself.

I looked into it. In 2021 council approved a program to keep stormwater out of our sewers, and the [staff report](https://esquimalt.ca.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?From=RSS&ID=30234&GUID=7B5124D6-CA57-4C69-B45D-1B978C3FFA9D) says the cost of work on private pipes "will be shared equally between the homeowner and the Township." What I cannot find is any public explanation of who qualifies, or whether it would help a couple like this one. I will be asking. And if the Township can't share the cost, it could at least offer to put the fee on the property tax bill so it can be paid off over several years.

## And one more

A neighbour who is a permanent resident, so not yet able to vote, said that if they could ask for one thing, it would be to finish the upgrades at Archie Browning sooner rather than later, because they want their kids skating regularly.

More doors this weekend!

dispatches.title: The noise, oh the noise! Can we better love our neighbours?
dispatches.summary: On Wednesday afternoon's doors, one chorus: keep to the Official Community Plan. Underneath it, years of construction noise, and a question about how a town cares for the people living next to its growth.
dispatches.body:
The residents I spoke with on Wednesday afternoon had one common chorus: please abide by the Official Community Plan, and permit no more than six storeys where that is what the plan says. Other themes were love, care and time. The restoration of Island Rail came up too, but I will leave that for a later post.

## What years of construction feel like

One older resident living beside a construction zone has a sensitivity to sound. For them, the difference between building six floors and building nine is not abstract. It is more months of noise cutting into their later years, and nine storeys of neighbours looking into a back yard they may never fully enjoy again. Their partner told me they spend six or more hours a day wearing noise‑cancelling headphones, and that after years of construction this has impacted the couple's communication with each other.

A parent of young children, also concerned about OCP adherence, told me that repeated rock blasting nearly pushed them to the brink of a mental‑health crisis. When everything in life is already too much, and we add years of blasting next door, we have created a real problem.

These are texture‑of‑life impacts stretched over long spans of time. Everyone I spoke with agreed that densification is important. But the impacts are viscerally felt. We can do better.

One pro‑density neighbour confessed, with heart‑warming Canadian self‑deprecation, that going to council over a project in their back yard was nimbyism, since they support density everywhere else. But this project was literally in their back yard, and it proposed to exceed the existing OCP.

## Green for grey

Another neighbour who shared the OCP concerns suggested that densification in one area should come with an expansion of enjoyable green space in another. In conversation we started calling it a Green‑for‑Grey Initiative. Developers might not only commit to conserving canopy on site but contribute to a pool for green‑space expansion and canopy conservation elsewhere in town. This could be a part of taking Esquimalt away from the current haphazard approach to development negotiations and fall in line with BC's new Amenity Cost Charge bylaw provisions under the Local Government Act. The devil will be in the details, but I broadly support Esquimalt adopting an Amenity Cost Charge bylaw. I've since written this up as [Proposal 03: Green for Grey](#proposal-03).

That neighbour mentioned a study on canopy and cooling, so I looked it up. [Research modelling Manchester in the UK](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169204613001916) found that adding five percent mature deciduous tree cover could lower average summer surface temperatures by about one degree. This falls in line with my commitment to forwarding a [Right to Cool bylaw](#dispatch-01) soon after taking office.

A focus on fostering green canopy is exciting, and it fits my ambition to see Esquimalt become a carbon‑negative community. If our canopy plan includes fast‑growing deciduous trees like bigleaf maple, and we treat prunings and the decadal replacement of trees not as wood waste but as contributions to long‑term carbon storage through pyrolysis, we start putting meaningful acreage to work on both urban cooling and atmospheric carbon removal. That is the sort of legacy infrastructure I would love to leave the next generations.

## Time as accessibility

A neighbour with a background in critical disability studies pointed out how much room there is to widen our approach to accessibility, starting with time. One low‑cost example: [in the Australian state of Victoria](https://transport.vic.gov.au/road-and-active-transport/road-rules-and-safety/permits/accessible-parking-permits), people with accessible parking permits may park for double the posted time. The last thing someone who struggles to keep up with ableist pacing needs is to be rushed by it. Of course, with Esquimalt's scantily enforced approach to parking such a policy would have less impact locally, but showing leadership in this regard and encouraging region‑wide adoption of such policies would be fantastic. I think our neighbour makes a good point, and I would be happy to add this to a list of proposals to bring to council.

## Housing, and a coalition of the pro‑active

One of the OCP‑concerned, pro‑density neighbours was most concerned about housing for people who are unhoused, and wondered what role Esquimalt could play. For the little historical context I have, I shared that a friend who used to run a social‑service agency told me that years ago they could call landlords in Esquimalt and find a place for someone struggling to keep a roof over their head. As Esquimalt gentrified, those opportunities all but dried up.

I mentioned the approach taken by the Woodward's redevelopment in Vancouver. Some echoes of that can be seen in Esquimalt Town Square, but I acknowledge that there is more thinking and working to be done. We agreed on two things. Esquimalt should stay a pro‑active community when it comes to people's right to housing. And no municipality in the region should be able to sit out while others carry the load, which is how many people here already feel about regional policing. Thinking of the good work and good spirit that Rainbow Kitchen and the United Church bring, we wondered what a regional approach might look like, not just to policing, but to poverty alleviation and to upholding rights like access to housing.

What I could commit to as a councillor is to work with established organisations while seeking out like‑minded people and organizations, churches, grassroots groups, and specific councillors and mayors across the region, and form a results‑oriented "coalition of the pro‑active" that brings tangible solutions to the housing challenges our local and regional neighbours face.

## Caring for the neighbours of a construction site

In a neighbourhood that has lived with construction noise for years, it was clear that if we want a low‑cortisol Esquimalt, we need to do a better job of caring for our neighbours when we choose to put them through years of disruption.

One off‑the‑cuff idea, which might also be a long‑term opportunity for a worker, community or entrepreneur‑owned business: encourage as much off‑site prefabrication as possible, through rezoning conditions and construction management plans, to cut on‑site noise, construction time and trades parking. Alongside that, consider a noise, time and neighbourhood wellbeing assessment that looks at the actual neighbours rather than an abstract receptor on a map.

We are a small enough community to do this with a human face. Neighbours who want to can tell us what they are dealing with, a noise sensitivity, a newborn, an autistic child who may be disproportionately affected, and the developer can be invited to be part of the care for that household, rather than cast in the adversarial good‑guy, bad‑guy roles so common in our culture and politics.

I could commit to knocking on the doors around proposed developments to understand the texture‑of‑life impacts before decisions are made, and to create pathways for developers to exercise care that reaches the actual people affected.

dispatches.title: The Lampson and Transit Road squeeze
dispatches.summary: Traffic on the Lampson and Transit Road corridor is bad and getting worse, and it is reaching into driveways, laneways and emergency response. What I heard on Tuesday evening's doors.
dispatches.body:
We cannot have a low‑cortisol Esquimalt while first responders struggle to get through traffic, children at play are put at risk by frustrated drivers hunting for shortcuts, and the interface between drivers and cyclists stays unfriendly. Tuesday evening's door knocks, along Lampson and the streets around Transit Road, pointed at exactly those pressure points.

## Lampson and Transit Road

For hours a day, some residents say it is nearly impossible to pull out of their own driveways. One neighbour described how, soon after the bike lanes went in, a barrier ended up blocking their ability to turn onto the street safely. Another chuckled, in dismay, at how many drivers they have watched get stuck on the barriers.

## The bike lanes: supported, but

Here is the finding that surprised me. All but one of the neighbours who raised concerns about the Lampson bike lanes identified as cyclists, most of whom use or used a bike for their daily commute. Every one of them said they broadly support bike lanes. Their objection was the concrete. One suggested that flexible delineators would have delivered the same protection while leaving room for drivers to pull aside and for residents to turn into their driveways. Everyone agreed they want roadways that are safe for bikes and drivers alike.

What I can commit to out of this is to check in with first responders first and foremost and to review how the bike lanes are working, with cyclists, drivers, and residents along the route.

## Emergency access

A commercial truck driver told me they once watched an emergency vehicle stuck for ten minutes in the area because cars could not pull to the side with the new barriers in place. That is one resident's account, and I want to know whether it reflects a pattern. I will check in with the ambulance station on Ellery and with the fire department to hear what emergency access looks like from their side.

That same driver asked for something simple: consult professional drivers when traffic decisions are made. From what they have seen on the ground, they said that it does not appear that is what is happening at present. They also wished for better morning transit to Langford, where they pick up their truck each day, and noted with approval that unlike James Bay, Esquimalt does not have Lime bikes filling loading zones. Raising transit ridership, they said, should be a priority. I agree.

## The Ellery laneway

One very specific concern: with the congestion of recent years, the laneway between Ellery and Colville has become a bypass route, and some drivers take it at speed. Children regularly play there. Neighbours asked for a speed bump or two to slow anyone attempting the shortcut. That is a small fix with a clear purpose, and I will push for it.

## The Blue Boat

A retired neighbour who cycled to the dockyard for decades remembered the social richness of the Blue Boat ride and argued it makes every kind of sense to bring it back. I've looked into it. The service only worked as a shuttle for people working on the base, not as public transit, and when it ended in 2012 it was reportedly carrying about 500 people a day who would otherwise have been driving alone. I've also read the [feasibility work on a public ferry between Royal Bay and Esquimalt](https://www.bcferries.com/web_image/h36/hb2/8851687997470.pdf), and I don't see that one flying.

A base‑employee shuttle is a different question. I can commit to speaking with base leadership to understand what stands in the way of bringing it back and, if there is a path, work with the right parties to reopen it.

## Trucks and yellow lines

Another neighbour walked me through how hard it is to turn a large truck around Colville, Transit and Lampson, fuel trucks especially at Transit Road. They also pointed out that some of the yellow curb lines are dated, and, pointing across the street at a parked car to make the point, it is clear that a number of residents just ignore them and park in front of them. A yellow‑line audit came up. That seems like a sensible, low‑cost ask. They also wanted clarity on the direction the Township plans to take with short‑term rentals.

## Park and bike

A neighbour described watching people arrive on their street each morning, park, and ride bikes into downtown, taking advantage of Esquimalt's free street parking. Their guess was Langford commuters. The concern was not acute, but there was a sense of Esquimalt being taken advantage of, and street parking is the most consistent concern I hear at any door. Some form of "except residents" parking restrictions on affected streets may make sense.

The pattern reminded me of my own commutes in Japan, first as an exchange student and later during my master's. One cheap bike to the train station, a train, and a second cheap bike from the station to school. Secure overnight bike parking is what made it effortless. People are already treating Esquimalt as their station. Once the Island Rail Corridor runs again from the West Shore to Vic West, we can make that impulse work for everyone, with secure bike parking and bike‑share stations in the right places, instead of on someone's street.

## Odds and ends

Property taxes came up once. The resident who raised them noted that they are a concern for some but said they personally felt they were within reason. And one neighbour noted that their favourite Esquimalt festival was Ribfest.

dispatches.title: A regional policing plan
dispatches.summary: We have a regional theatre service. Why not a regional policing plan? What two neighbours said about policing, what the reports say, and the first step I would bring to council.
dispatches.body:
## We have a regional theatre service. Why not a regional policing plan?

At the Labour Day Picnic, before I had decided to run for council, I had an interesting conversation with members of IATSE who work in local theatre. Having some experience myself with the uncertainty of arts funding, I asked how people in the sector were doing. They were enthusiastic about the stability they expect from the Capital Regional District's newly adopted [Performing Arts Facilities Service](https://www.crd.ca/news/crd-board-adopts-bylaw-establish-performing-arts-facilities-service).

It is a real regional accomplishment. Municipalities across the region have agreed to share responsibility for the Royal Theatre, the McPherson Playhouse and the Charlie White Theatre, facilities that serve people well beyond the municipalities they happen to sit in. The service starts in 2027.

Policing is a far bigger undertaking, with a budget many times the size and rules set by the Police Act. The mechanism won't necessarily transfer, but the principle might: the region can pull together on something of shared value when it decides to. It struck me as a hopeful reference point for the many areas where better regional coordination is essential, policing among them.

Policing came up on my first day speaking with neighbours. One person talked about how reassuring it is to live close to police and fire services. Another raised a concern I have heard repeatedly in Esquimalt: that Esquimalt taxpayers carry part of the cost of policing problems concentrated in Victoria which Saanich, Oak Bay and Central Saanich with their own departments and West Shore with the RCMP participate less.

Noting the RCMP's history with First Nations, that neighbour was wary of an RCMP alternative. In any event, the Township's [2023 Policing Service Delivery Model Review](https://www.esquimalt.ca/public-safety/policing-esquimalt) concluded that a full switch to the RCMP was not a realistic option under the federal rules and agreements in place, and that RCMP facility standards would require more investment in Esquimalt facilities than is reasonably expected in the foreseeable future..

So I shared with our neighbour about the regional performing‑arts agreement and asked: what could a regional policing equivalent look like?

## In some ways, regional policing already exists

Greater Victoria already shares a surprising amount of policing: integrated teams for domestic violence, youth, mental‑health crisis response, canine services and more. But it is a patchwork rather than a plan, and commitment can be fickle. [VicPD's 2026 budget documents](https://ehq-production-canada.s3.ca-central-1.amazonaws.com/d368f921219180251bf081f172b200af90690382/original/1764018789/6f55bbca0097b871f5fab52c08d35100_Report_Victoria%20Police%202026%20Budget.pdf) report that Central Saanich withdrew from the Mobile Youth Services Team, the Regional Domestic Violence Unit and the Integrated Mobile Crisis Response Team in 2025, and that West Shore RCMP was scheduled to withdraw from some of those services in 2026 and from the domestic‑violence unit in 2027. 

That is not an argument for any particular institutional model. It illustrates the problem: we have some regional policing, but no stable regional policing plan.

## We certainly haven't lacked for studies

Greater Victoria has debated regional policing for decades. Regionalization studies go back at least to the late 1970s, and the Justice Institute of British Columbia's [bibliography on police regionalization](https://www.jibc.ca/sites/default/files/2020-03/library-police-regionalization-jibc-2016.pdf) points to a substantial body of work on the question.

Esquimalt in particular has spent years examining alternatives. The Township is currently exploring an Esquimalt police department supported by specialized services from neighbouring agencies, while stating that its long‑term goal is regional policing. In July 2026, [Council directed](https://esquimalt.ca.legistar.com/ViewReport.ashx?M=R&N=Text&GID=5&ID=37932&GUID=079A9F38-C5AF-44D3-BF0E-2E229F5E67A5&Title=Legislation+Text) that the incoming 2026 to 2030 Council receive a comprehensive policing orientation and strategic discussion. There is, in other words, no shortage of paper.

I am trying to track down one document in particular: the 1985 proposal by the Victoria‑area police chiefs for Greater Victoria Regional Police Services. I want to understand what they thought could be shared or consolidated forty years ago, why it did not happen, and whether any of those lessons still hold. If anyone has a copy, please share it. Otherwise, once I locate it through the Justice Institute library, and if I have permission to scan it, I will post it here.

## I don't pretend to know the final model

A single regional police service might ultimately make sense. Stronger integrated services might make more sense. There may be a model, like one proposed in recent years, in which a smaller Esquimalt service buys specialized functions regionally. Governance, accountability and cost‑sharing will probably matter more than what is painted on the side of the cars.

We do not need to settle that before agreeing on something more basic: Greater Victoria needs a coherent regional policing plan. A plan would identify which challenges are truly regional, which services are best delivered locally and which shared, how regional services should be governed and funded, and how municipalities can stop repeatedly rebuilding, or walking away from, the same collaborations.

Esquimalt Council cannot answer those questions alone. Any serious process needs Victoria, Saanich, Oak Bay and the other municipalities; the Province and the police boards; regional health and social‑service partners; with special care and attention given to ensuring meaningful involvement of local First Nations, whose historical relationship with policing has been, as the neighbour rightly pointed out, fraught.

My contribution would be to do the homework. I will be the nerd on council who reads all of the reports. I will keep asking questions, listen to police leadership and front‑line members, to the local First Nations, and to Esquimalt residents and community organizations, and push for a system in which Esquimalt gets good policing and bears a fair share of the costs of the regional services we all benefit from. I am less attached to the organizational chart than to getting the result right.

**A first step I could bring forward:** a motion asking Council to invite the neighbouring councils and police boards to a joint session on a regional policing plan, building on the policing orientation the incoming Council has already been directed to receive.

There are already institutions building relationships across departmental lines. The Greater Victoria Police Foundation is one. Those relationships matter, because regional cooperation depends not only on funding formulas and governance agreements but on trust between the people involved. Leaning into the bodies that build that trust is part of the work.

## Policing is only one part of community safety

A regional policing plan should not be confused with a complete community‑safety plan. There is another side of safety, much closer to home: the strength of the relationships around us. A community where people who are struggling can find food, company, mental‑health support, addiction services and a place to belong is a safer community too.

In Esquimalt, Rainbow Kitchen and the United Church at Admirals and Lyall come to mind as examples of that spirit: making love the foundation of our community's safety and flourishing. The bureaucratic work of policing governance and budgets will be difficult and slow, and we need to do it. At the same time, we can keep building the kind of community in which fewer people fall through the cracks in the first place.

One small initiative I would like your feedback on: the Township could propose an Esquimalt‑convened community‑safety session at the next [Victoria Forum](https://victoriaforum.ca/), the gathering co‑hosted by the Senate of Canada, the University of Victoria and Royal Roads University that brings leaders and community members together on governance challenges. Convening that discussion would be one way to gather regional, provincial, federal and First Nations political will behind the regional policing plan we need.

Please let me know what you think.

dispatches.title: Day one at the door
dispatches.summary: Parking, child care, the right to cool, and the value of community stake in developments were the big issues on the first day of my door knocking.
dispatches.body:
## Child care

Child care in general is a big challenge for young parents. The lack of child care spots was a general challenge noted by parents, with some noting how they have their young children on multiple waitlists as they struggle to balance work and child care. More specifically, lower‑income parents who work evenings and weekends noted the lack of child care services that accommodate their schedules. This was particularly acute for new immigrant families, who have limited local social networks and face linguistic, cultural and, let's call them bureaucratic‑maze barriers to accessing local services.

My reflection on this is that we need to better equip our community so that child care meets the diverse needs of our residents. This does not all have to be a municipal or other level of government responsibility or expense, but there is a big role for the municipality to play, in collaboration with other service providers, as an efficient facilitator, coordinator and advocate.  If anyone has a specific proposal they would like to share, please let me know and maybe there is an initiative we can push forward.

## Street parking

There were strong arguments that Esquimalt wildly lacks street parking, with the point made that if a major construction project were to come to town, it would squeeze residents out of their preferred homefront spots. Those homefront spots are clearly very highly valued!

One resident recounted how, when they moved into their Esquimalt home a number of years ago, if they happened to park in a spot right in front of their own house that turned out to be a neighbour's long‑time preferred spot, they would find bags of dog poop and grass clippings on their vehicle. Rather than communicate their preferences directly, the neighbour communicated via poop bags and yard waste. It was only when the issue was finally raised in person that they realised what was going on.

Some residents felt that other homeowners were guarding the street in front of their homes while filling their own driveways and front lawns with boats, RVs and other space‑occupying paraphernalia. Parking is clearly an issue for Esquimalt residents.

## Getting to and from the base

One resident had an interesting twist on parking. They alerted me to the Base's policy of allowing free parking because Esquimalt has no pay parking. In Halifax, they noted, the base charges for parking on par with local rates. I looked it up, and it turns out it is a thing: DND's policy is to charge for parking at local market rates, and if the local market is free, it is free on base too. This resident suggested that bringing in nominal paid parking, perhaps with street‑specific passes for residents and paid parking for non‑residents, might have some impact on base employees' transit use. Though, they noted, bringing back the Blue Boat (the ferry from the base to Colwood) or reviving the Island Rail Corridor, at least to Langford, would be the real solution.

Another long‑time resident, born and raised here, who worked at the dockyard and is now retired, recounted how the Blue Boat took loads of cars off our constrained roadways. When the Blue Boat was privatised and became a paid service, it fell apart, and we started to get the congestion we know all too well today. I looked it up, and that does appear to be exactly what happened. Here is some follow‑on reading for anyone interested:

- [Celebrating what the Blue Boat provided, 2009 (page 10)](https://ufdcimages.uflib.ufl.edu/AA/00/06/78/39/00060/09-14-2009.pdf)
- [Blue Boat to cease, Lookout Newspaper](https://lookoutnewspaper.com/blue-boat-to-cease/)
- [Goodbye Blue Boat service, Lookout Newspaper](https://lookoutnewspaper.com/goodbye-blue-boat-service/)
- [Solve the Colwood Crawl, Capital Daily, 2022](https://www.capitaldaily.ca/news/solve-the-colwood-crawl)

The Capital Daily piece is a particularly interesting and informative overview of the breadth of proposals that have come along. Reading it made me reflect that no matter how much highway widening you do, it isn't going to have much impact on the stretch of Admirals that matters most to residents: the bit from Esquimalt Road to the Island Highway. That stretch is exactly what my first proposal, [the Esquimalt Free Ride](#proposal-01), is aimed at.

## The right to cool

The right to cool was my "you learn something new every day" piece, and I am grateful to the resident who brought it to my attention. This one is important. As heatwaves become more and more a part of our lived experience, tenants' access to coolness is essential. It makes sense to me that no resident should be living with indoor temperatures above 26 degrees.

[Ecotrust Canada's 2025 report](https://ecotrust.ca/latest/research/safe-temperatures-in-bc-rental-housing-municipal-and-provincial-policy-pathways-2025/) lays out the sorts of bylaws municipalities can bring in. According to their website, New Westminster brought in a bylaw in June requiring landlords to keep at least one living space in an occupied rental unit at a safe temperature of 26°C or lower at night. That sounds abundantly reasonable to me, and I will work to table a proposal of this sort soon after taking office. If I am elected, hound me, and hold me and the rest of council to account on this. With an El Niño possibly on the way, there is a real chance that the summer of 2027 is the summer we need this bylaw in place.

## Community stake in developments

One resident drew a very interesting contrast between two recent developments. The Proxima development, they quipped, was all about getting as close to the road as possible, eliminating not only old trees but also a bus bay, and making, in their view, the Lampson and Esquimalt Road intersection more dangerous. They contrasted this with the Esquimalt Town Square development where, they posited, because the community had a stake, an important old tree was kept and the space was made breathable and vibrant, a real addition to the community. This conversation was food for thought, and I think it makes sense for us to reflect on what role community stake can play in future developments that will call Esquimalt home.

I particularly like the notion of development as a collaboration between community and entrepreneurs, rather than a wrestling match in which a singularly focused developer wrangles as much as they can out of a multi‑focused municipality to maximise the profitability of their project. Finding paths, as with the Esquimalt Town Square, where the community shares a stake in a development is interesting to contemplate. This would take more study and consideration, but I wonder whether an approach where the community has a stake may be relevant when it comes time to redevelop the Country Grocer complex.

## Small fixes

I also heard calls for stop signs at the complex intersection of Munro and Fraser, and a call from a young parent for greater traffic calming on Sturdee.

This is what I am hearing so far. Stay tuned, I will report more as I keep knocking on doors.

proposals.heading: Drafts for council's consideration
proposals.intro: Written so a councillor could table them. Each one says what we'd try, who we'd partner with, and how we'd know if it worked.

items.title: The Esquimalt Free Ride
items.subtitle: An Esquimalt Defence and Employment Mobility Pilot: free regional transit for people who work here, with more buses timed to shift changes.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text:
Esquimalt hosts an extraordinary concentration of regional employment, including CFB Esquimalt, the home of Canada's Pacific Fleet, and the Esquimalt Graving Dock and Victoria Shipyards. Thousands of workers travel each day through a small number of constrained transportation corridors, contributing to recurring congestion on Admirals, Esquimalt, Lampson and connecting roads.

Significant expansion of roadway capacity would be costly, disruptive and unlikely to provide a durable solution.

sections.heading: The proposal
sections.text:
Esquimalt should seek provincial and federal support for an Esquimalt Defence and Employment Mobility Pilot, or an Esquimalt Regional Free Ride program.

For an initial 18‑ to 24‑month demonstration period, people employed in Esquimalt would be eligible for free regional transit, supported by increased service timed to major employment shifts and targeted transit‑priority improvements. An alternative would be to make the designated commuter routes along Admirals Road, Esquimalt Road and Lampson Street free for all riders.

The program would be undertaken in partnership with the Victoria Regional Transit Commission, BC Transit, the Capital Regional District, CFB Esquimalt, major employers and senior levels of government, with the option of extending it for up to five years if it demonstrates significant reductions in automobile commuting and congestion.

The project would test whether removing the cost of transit while improving its convenience can substantially reduce peak‑hour vehicle traffic without widening Esquimalt's constrained road network.

sections.heading: A second benefit for the base
sections.text: For CFB Esquimalt in particular, the project would provide greater transportation redundancy and operational resilience for Canada's Pacific naval establishment. In an era of increasingly sophisticated asymmetric threats, natural disasters and other potential disruptions, reducing dependence on a small number of congested automobile corridors would strengthen the ability of defence personnel and other critical workers to reliably reach and leave their workplaces.

sections.heading: How we'd know it worked
sections.text:
Success would be measured against existing traffic counts and commute data, including changes in:

- single‑occupancy vehicle trips
- transit ridership
- peak travel times
- greenhouse‑gas emissions
- employee commute reliability
- cost per automobile trip removed

sections.heading: Paying for it
sections.text: There are a number of established federal and provincial programs that Esquimalt could apply to in order to fund this. Bringing that outside investment into town is platform item 8.

glance.label: Pilot length
glance.value: 18 to 24 months, extendable to five years if it works

glance.label: Who rides free
glance.value: People employed in Esquimalt, or everyone on the Admirals, Esquimalt Rd and Lampson commuter routes

glance.label: Comes with
glance.value: More buses timed to shift changes, plus transit‑priority improvements on the corridors

glance.label: Partners
glance.value: Victoria Regional Transit Commission, BC Transit, CRD, CFB Esquimalt, major employers, Province of BC, Government of Canada

glance.label: Funding
glance.value: Existing federal and provincial programs

glance.label: Platform items
glance.value:
1 · Fix the daily traffic jam
3 · Easier to walk and ride
8 · More outside investment

items.title: A Right to Cool
items.subtitle: A safe‑temperature standard for Esquimalt rental homes: tenants may always use cooling devices, and every occupied rental unit has at least one room that stays at 26°C or lower on hot nights.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text:
The 2021 heat dome was the deadliest weather event in Canadian history. The BC Coroners Service attributed 619 deaths to it across the province, and found that 98 percent of those people died indoors, most of them older, many living alone, in homes without adequate cooling. Thirty‑three of them lived in New Westminster.

Heat waves are becoming a regular part of life here. A large share of Esquimalt households rent, many in older apartment buildings built with no thought of cooling. Tenants cannot renovate their own homes, and some leases still forbid air conditioners. New buildings are already covered: since 2024 the BC Building Code requires every new home to have one living space designed to stay at or below 26°C. Existing rental housing, where the risk is greatest, has no such protection.

sections.heading: Why the summer of 2027
sections.text:
In its latest outlook, [NOAA reports that El Niño has formed and is strengthening](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters), with a greater than 90 percent chance of a very strong event through the fall and winter of 2026 to 2027, and conditions expected to persist into spring.

That matters for timing. The year that follows a strong El Niño has repeatedly been among the hottest on record globally: 1998, 2016 and 2024 all followed one. El Niño does not cause any particular heat wave, and nobody can promise what next July will bring to Esquimalt. But it loads the dice, and 2027 is the year the dice are most heavily loaded.

A bylaw adopted in 2028 would arrive a summer late. That is why this proposal asks staff to report back in time for adoption before April 2027, and why the first step, guaranteeing tenants the right to use their own cooling devices, should be in force before the first warm week of next year.

sections.heading: The proposal
sections.text:
Follow the two steps New Westminster took, in the same order.

- **Step one, the right to cool.** A landlord may not prohibit a tenant from installing or using a portable cooling device. New Westminster adopted this in 2025.
- **Step two, a safe temperature.** In every occupied rental unit, at least one living space, not counting the kitchen or bathroom, must not exceed an average of 26°C between 8pm and 8am, from April 1 to October 31. [New Westminster adopted this on June 8, 2026](https://www.newwestcity.ca/cooling-requirements).

The standard does not require air conditioning or a heat pump. Owners choose how to meet it: shading, window film, thermal curtains, ceiling fans, air sealing, portable units, or a heat pump where it makes sense. The rule is about the result, not the equipment.

sections.heading: How it would work in Esquimalt
sections.text:
Esquimalt already licenses rental apartment properties under the [Business Licence and Regulation Bylaw, No. 3144](https://esquimalt.ca.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EC763462-8CB9-4BC0-80C9-4D5003264CCC&ID=62029&M=F), adopted in 2024. New Westminster used exactly that kind of bylaw as its vehicle, so the legal path is proven and no new bureaucracy is needed.

- **Timeline.** Bring the amendment forward early in the term so that step one is in force for the summer of 2027, and step two applies from April 1, 2027 with a compliance‑first approach in its first season.
- **Compliance before tickets.** As in New Westminster, a complaint leads first to a conversation and a compliance plan with reasonable timelines. Fines are the backstop. New Westminster's range from $200 to $750 and may be issued daily.
- **Exemptions.** Where an owner has made reasonable efforts and the building simply cannot meet the standard, a report from a registered professional supports a two‑year exemption, after which the question is revisited.
- **Help for owners.** Pair the rule with a plain‑language cooling guide, encouragement of building cooling audits, and active promotion of provincial and utility rebates for heat pumps and efficiency upgrades in rental buildings.

sections.heading: Protecting tenants from the cost
sections.text: A cooling rule must not become a reason for rents to jump or for tenants to be displaced. Two things follow. Staff should report on how to keep compliance costs modest, which is why the standard covers one room and leaves the method open. And Council should ask the Province to write a right to cool into the Residential Tenancy Act, with protections against passing retrofit costs to tenants, as [Ecotrust Canada's 2025 report](https://ecotrust.ca/latest/research/safe-temperatures-in-bc-rental-housing-municipal-and-provincial-policy-pathways-2025/) recommends.

sections.heading: How we'd know it worked
sections.text:
- Complaints received, and how many were resolved through compliance plans without fines
- Rental buildings that have completed a cooling audit
- Exemptions requested and granted
- Heat‑related emergency calls from rental buildings during heat warnings, compared year over year
- A short tenant survey after the first full summer

sections.heading: Draft motion
sections.text:
THAT Council direct staff to report back, in time for adoption before April 2027, with amendments to the Business Licence and Regulation Bylaw, No. 3144, modelled on the City of New Westminster's Business Regulations and Licensing (Rental Units) Bylaw amendments of 2025 and 2026, that would (1) prevent owners of rental units from prohibiting tenants' use of cooling devices, and (2) require that at least one living space in each occupied rental unit not exceed an average of 26°C between 8pm and 8am from April 1 to October 31; and

THAT the report include a compliance‑first enforcement approach, an exemption process, supports for property owners, and options to protect tenants from resulting rent increases; and

THAT the Mayor write to the Minister of Housing asking that a right to cool be added to the Residential Tenancy Act.

glance.label: The standard
glance.value: One living space at or below an average of 26°C, 8pm to 8am

glance.label: When
glance.value: April 1 to October 31 each year

glance.label: Also
glance.value: Landlords cannot prohibit tenants' cooling devices

glance.label: Why now
glance.value: A very strong El Niño raises the odds of a record‑hot 2027

glance.label: Legal vehicle
glance.value: Business Licence and Regulation Bylaw No. 3144, which already licenses rental apartments

glance.label: Modelled on
glance.value: New Westminster, adopted 2025 and June 2026

glance.label: Enforcement
glance.value: Complaint‑driven; compliance plan first, fines as backstop

glance.label: Platform item
glance.value: 9 · Bring in a right to cool

items.title: Green for Grey
items.subtitle: When a neighbourhood takes on more density, it gets more green in return: parkland, canopy and cool public space, funded by growth through clear, published charges instead of one‑off negotiations.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: Esquimalt is growing, and most people I speak with support that. What they object to is absorbing the noise, the height and the traffic of densification and seeing nothing come back to their street. At the same time, Esquimalt is one of the few growing municipalities in the region with no Development Cost Charge bylaw and no Amenity Cost Charge bylaw. Growth‑related needs are paid for through property taxes, borrowing and grants, and what a developer contributes is settled project by project. That is slow, unpredictable for builders, and opaque for neighbours.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every increase in grey, meaning storeys, units and pavement, is matched by an increase in green that the affected neighbourhood can actually enjoy. A neighbour coined the phrase at the door, and the principle is simple: growth pays for green, by formula, in the open.

sections.heading: The right tool for each part
sections.text:
BC law gives municipalities separate tools, and they cannot overlap. Green for Grey uses each for what it is allowed to do.

- **Parkland, through Development Cost Charges.** Acquiring and improving parkland is a DCC purpose. A DCC program can fund new pocket parks and the improvement of existing ones, directed to the neighbourhoods absorbing the most growth.
- **Community amenities, through Amenity Cost Charges.** The [ACC provisions](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/governments/local-governments/finance/local-government-development-financing/amenity-cost-charges) added to the Local Government Act in 2023 fund capital amenities that serve growing areas, such as recreation and community facilities, child care space and public gathering places. Staff and legal counsel should confirm which green public‑realm features qualify.
- **Canopy, through tree protection and development permits.** Retaining mature trees on site, replacing those removed, and paying into a tree fund where replacement on site is impossible.
- **In the interim, through rezoning conditions.** Until the bylaws exist, Council can ask for the same outcomes when it considers rezonings, applied consistently rather than case by case.

sections.heading: Why canopy matters
sections.text: [Research modelling Manchester in the UK](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169204613001916) found that adding five percent mature deciduous tree cover could lower average summer surface temperatures by about one degree. Shade is public cooling infrastructure. It complements a [Right to Cool](#proposal-02) inside our homes with cooler streets outside them, and it serves my goal of a carbon‑removing town: fast‑growing canopy, with prunings and replacements treated as long‑term carbon storage rather than waste.

sections.heading: Principles
sections.text:
- **By formula, not by haggling.** Published charges give builders certainty and neighbours confidence.
- **Green lands near the grey.** Funds are spent in or near the neighbourhoods taking on the density.
- **Don't tax the housing we most need.** Use the Act's power to waive or reduce charges for non‑profit, supportive and affordable rental housing.
- **Report in public.** The Act already requires an annual report on these funds by June 30. Make it readable, and map what was built where.

sections.heading: How we'd know it worked
sections.text:
- Square metres of new or improved park and public green space per hundred new homes
- Tree canopy cover, measured against a baseline and a target
- Share of funds spent within the neighbourhoods where they were collected
- Time from rezoning application to decision, as a check that certainty is speeding things up

sections.heading: Draft motion
sections.text:
THAT the impact assessment on Development Cost Charge and Amenity Cost Charge bylaws requested by Council in January 2026 include a Green for Grey component, identifying (a) a parkland acquisition and improvement program fundable through Development Cost Charges and directed to neighbourhoods absorbing growth, (b) the green and public‑realm amenities eligible for funding through Amenity Cost Charges under the Local Government Act, and (c) waivers or reductions for non‑profit, supportive and affordable rental housing; and

THAT staff report on establishing a baseline measurement of Esquimalt's tree canopy, a canopy target, and a tree fund for cases where trees removed through development cannot be replaced on site; and

THAT, until such bylaws are adopted, staff propose an interim policy so that green‑space and canopy contributions are sought consistently when Council considers rezoning applications.

about.heading: An Esquimalt dad who knows the town at stroller speed, and now scooter speed.
about.body:
My campaign started with my son. He is almost five, and he has been persistently insisting that something be done about the bumpiness of our community's sidewalks. I got to know the unique texture of the Saxe Point and Rockheights neighbourhoods first at stroller and more recently at scooter speed, and he has a point.

We moved here in 2021, and I am convinced that this town, daily traffic jam aside, is the best place to live for anyone who wants to raise children in a warm, convenient, walkable, park‑rich community with fun festivals and vibrant events. It is a place I will happily age into, with down‑to‑earth friends nearby and grocery stores and other services a short stroll away.

Before Esquimalt, I lived for extended periods on three continents, from an ethnically diverse farming village in eastern Croatia to some of Asia's largest and most complex cities. Along the way I interned at the Pearson Peacekeeping Training Centre, served as Coordinator for International Relations for a small Japanese municipality, where I coordinated affairs for the Cameroonian national football team for the FIFA World Cup, organized large‑scale art exhibitions in Korea, and ran the Okanagan's largest arts centre. More recently I have helped international partners build disaster‑preparedness training tools and consulted for environmentally progressive forestry transformation and waste‑management projects.

My son and I are regulars at our parks and recreation facilities, and I am grateful for the shops, restaurants and amenities close by. I see Esquimalt as a community where friends of all ages and backgrounds can have fun, feel included, know there is support when they need it, and be joy‑filled as we work together to make this an even better place to be.
facts: Lives in Saxe Point, in an apartment, with his almost‑five‑year‑old son
Gets around by foot, scooter, transit and car share
Regular at Esquimalt's parks and rec facilities

involved.heading: Easy ways to help
involved.intro: This is a neighbour‑powered campaign. A sign in a window or an hour on a Saturday goes a long way in a town this size.

cards.title: Wear a pin
cards.text: A campaign pin for your jacket or bag, free, and I'll drop it by. Lawn signs cost $50 apiece, so they go up as contributions come in: chip in $50, say you'd like one, and it's yours.
cards.subject: I'd like a pin

cards.title: Knock doors with me
cards.text: Join a door‑knocking shift. You don't need to be an expert; you need to like talking to neighbours.
cards.subject: I'd like to volunteer

cards.title: Host a kitchen‑table chat
cards.text: Invite a few neighbours over and I'll come listen. Coffee optional, opinions welcome.
cards.subject: Let's host a chat

cards.title: Chip in
cards.text: A few dollars pays for signs and printing. Every contribution follows Elections BC rules, and the whole thing stays neighbour‑sized.

donate.heading: Chip in to a neighbour‑powered campaign.
donate.intro: Every dollar is spent in Esquimalt, and $50 pays for one lawn sign, so if you'd like one on your lawn, say so in the form below. Local campaign contributions in BC follow strict rules set by Elections BC, so please read the checklist before you give.
rules: You are a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, and you live in British Columbia.
You are giving your own money. Contributions from businesses, unions, organizations, or on someone else's behalf are not allowed.
You have not given more than **$1,429.70** in total to this campaign in 2026. That is the legal limit per person.
You are fine with your name and amount being published by Elections BC if you give **$100 or more**. This is required by law.
You understand there is no tax receipt for local election contributions.
donate.payNote: Credit or debit card through a secure payment page.
donate.fine: Contributions are received by Tyler Russell, financial agent, and deposited to the campaign account. Anonymous contributions are limited to $50 in total and cannot be made online. A contribution the campaign cannot legally accept will be returned within 30 days. Questions about the rules: Elections BC, 1‑800‑661‑8683, or [elections.bc.ca](https://elections.bc.ca/local-elections/making-a-campaign-contribution/).
donate.formHeading: Tell the financial agent who you are
donate.formIntro: The law requires a record of every contributor's full name and residential address. Fill this in when you send your contribution, whichever way you send it.
attest: I am a Canadian citizen or permanent resident and a resident of British Columbia.
This contribution is from my own money and is not being reimbursed by anyone.
With this contribution, my total to this campaign in 2026 is $1,429.70 or less.
donate.formNote: Goes to the financial agent only. Not published, except as Elections BC requires for contributions of $100 or more.

updates.heading: What I'm hearing, as I hear it.
updates.intro: I'm knocking on doors across Esquimalt and writing up what neighbours tell me, by theme and never by name, along with what I'd do about it. Here are the latest.
